report.summary: Deferred imports break cycles but cause delayed ImportError, performance overhead, and hidden dependency graphs. CI visibility requires exhaustive path import testing, import hook tracing, and static cycle detection.
risks: Runtime overhead from repeated importlib lookups in hot paths
Delayed discovery of missing modules until seldom-used code paths executed
Potential circular import errors re-emerging under specific call sequences
Static analysis tools may not detect dynamically evaluated imports
Windows-specific import quirks (e.g., case insensitivity) may complicate tracing
todos: Implement CI workflow that invokes all registered agent entry-points to trigger deferred imports and captures import errors
Add custom pytest fixture that wraps imports to log and assert no circular import exceptions
Integrate import-linter or custom pylint rule to flag modules using deferred imports for review
Refactor critical cycles using dependency injection or interfaces to eliminate deferred imports
Monitor import time during performance tests to identify hot-deferred-imports

handoff.suggestion: Daedalus should add a CI job that dynamically discovers and calls every agent's main function in a sandbox, catching ImportError/ModuleNotFoundError, complemented by a custom import hook that detects attempted circular imports by tracking partially initialized modules, and use coverage to ensure all deferred import sites are exercised.

name: q09-deferred-import-cycles
question: When a Python codebase uses function-local (deferred) imports to break import cycles, what are the documented failure modes at scale, and what techniques make the resulting runtime cycles visible in CI rather than only under manual graph analysis?
